<span class="html-render">Should writers use AI? Itâ€™s a topic that has generated frenzied discussion. Recently, Washington Post columnist Megan McArdle <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/04/05/artificial-intelligence-chatbot-writing-ethics/" target="_blank" rel="">kicked up a storm</a> when she wrote on X that she <a href="https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/04/09/opinion/journalism-industry-ai-tools-writers/" target="_blank" rel="">uses AI</a> for such tasks as transcribing interviews, analyzing her arguments, and fact-checking. Critics accused her of <a href="https://x.com/cwjones89/status/2037604786351067429" target="_blank" rel="">outsourcing her thinking</a> and told her to <a href="https://x.com/rbarrettfox/status/2037743340762841543" target="_blank" rel="">find a new job</a>. A Rutgers philosophy professor even <a href="https://x.com/BenBurgis/status/2037737365356310961" target="_blank" rel="">said</a> that â€œin a healthier media culture, an admission like this would at the very least get her fired.â€ One wonders what he means by *at the very least* and what kind of punishment he has in mind as a maximum.</span>

<span class="html-render">Yet the arguments one can make against her use of AI also apply to other forms of technology that are widely considered acceptable. In fact, I would go one step further than McArdle and say that there is nothing inherently wrong with writers using AI to compose text. The only way it would be unethical is if writers fail to disclose it, because people have an obligation to disclose information that publishers or readers might find relevant. Since I can write fast and well enough not to benefit much from AI writing, and because it would be against The Boston Globeâ€™s rules anyway, I did not use AI to write this piece. But I would encourage publications to avoid blanket rules against such a practice for those who need it. (I did use AI to check spelling and grammar before submitting my draft.)</span>

<span class="html-render">The arguments against using the basic functions of AI that McArdle brings up are easy to dispense with. We already have widely accepted tools to look up articles and find grammatical errors. Theyâ€™re called Google and spell-check. No one has a problem with either of them. Why would it be illegitimate to use a platform that effectively combines them?</span>

<span class="html-render">Regarding fact-checking, people have pointed to large language modelsâ€™ tendency to hallucinate information. This is an argument against relying *solely* on AI as a fact-checker, but little more. Recently, there was a controversy when it turned out that UK researcher Matt Goodwin included <a href="https://bylinetimes.com/2026/03/23/mattgpt-the-sorry-tale-of-matt-goodwins-ai-assisted-fake-quote-filled-new-book/" target="_blank" rel="">fabricated quotes</a> in his new book, which many thought was evidence he got them from AI. The problem, however, isnâ€™t which tool delivered these quotes to Goodwin but the fact that they were not real. If Google turns up a fake news website and a person cites it, we do not condemn the entire concept of a search engine. We chide the researcher for making a mistake. Thereâ€™s no excuse for an author today to not understand that information uncovered by LLMs needs to be traced back to an original source. In fact, those familiar with AI are aware that to uncover a hallucination, it usually requires nothing more than simply asking the LLM itself for a source, at which point it will admit that it was wrong. </span>

<span class="html-render">Can we take this one step further? While many will go to bat for AI fact-checkers or research assistants, few will defend someone using an LLM to write a column and then putting their name on it. I agree that if the outlet you are writing for has a rule against the practice or there is an analogous ethical consideration, you should not do it. But I would also argue that we should move toward a norm of accepting writers incorporating AI into their work as long as the normal standards of quality are met.</span>

<span class="html-render">We can understand why with a thought experiment. Imagine that at some point, people begin to notice a young writer with brilliant insights into public policy questions. No one can find factual or logical errors in his articles. But then he says every piece he has ever written was based on a draft originally created by ChatGPT in response to his prompts. At that point, should we decide that this personâ€™s work, which we all appreciated before the scandal, is worthless? Should he be shunned in public life?</span>

<span class="html-render">I would say not, and I hope the reader would agree. Writing is a skill. I can put together a newspaper op-ed in less than an hour, while I know others who need one or more days. Many people wouldnâ€™t have the ability to compose a respectable column no matter how much time you gave them. Some who are terrible writers might nonetheless have ideas that are worth hearing. On what basis should they be excluded from sharing those ideas because they lack this one skill? We do not care whether an author types up a research paper while using reading glasses to overcome a natural deficiency. What matters is whether the information they provide is factual, interesting, and logically coherent. A lack of writing skills should be seen the same way.</span>

<span class="html-render">The concerns about AI of course run deeper. People wonder whether such tools can harm our ability to develop thinking skills. But itâ€™s not obvious why writing itself is the process that makes people think better. If we stick to the principles of judging arguments and ideas by meritocratic standards, we can do that regardless of whether an author used LLMs for the writing. It is still a lot of work to figure out whether the information an LLM gives you is true and whether the arguments that it puts together are coherent and important enough to publish. You can criticize an author who uses AI for making illogical arguments or getting facts wrong just as much as you can criticize one who writes â€œnaturallyâ€ and does those things. The standards themselves are what matter, not the exact division of labor between man and machine in producing a work. </span>

<span class="html-render">The fact of the matter is that wealthier and more established authors already have ghostwriters and research assistants. Some of us without great wealth have natural writing talent that similarly puts us at an advantage. AI can be seen as a leveler. Although there may be a connection between writing well and thinking well, the correlation is far from perfect. I do not believe that people who do not write as well and as fast as I do should be excluded from public discourse any more than those who need glasses should not be able to benefit from scientific papers written in a small font. </span>

<span class="html-render">Many of the concerns expressed in the AI debate are legitimate. We cannot simply outsource our thinking to LLMs, any more than we should use Google by simply clicking on the first search result we find when researching a topic and taking what it says as gospel. But with other tools, we realize that increases in efficiency are generally good, even as we must remain on the lookout for ways in which they can degrade our understanding of the world. AI is a much more powerful tool for research than any that has come before. That certainly increases potential dangers, but it also opens up new possibilities of a public discourse that is more rational, grounded in facts, and inclusive. </span>
